endorsements.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Use formats and languages accessible to intended end users

endorsements.title: Chatting Beyond ChatGPT: Advancing Equity Through AI-Driven Language Interpretation
endorsements.quote: Lastly, providers must be trained in using the resources.

endorsements.title: Legal, ethical, and policy challenges of artificial intelligence translation tools in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Comprehensive training of healthcare providers is also key.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether multilingual, multi-format training for AI users reduces misuse or misunderstanding, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on one international consensus guideline and one commentary.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Support comes from a consensus guideline (FUTURE-AI) and a commentary on AI translation tools, both of which rank as expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative study measures user errors by training language or format.

The hazard concerns users who do not speak the training language, yet no supplied study measures how often this occurs or whom it affects. Without data, a health system cannot tell whether staff with limited English proficiency, or patients using patient-facing tools, face higher misuse rates than other users.

FUTURE-AI states that developers should use formats and languages accessible to intended end users. The translation-tools commentary calls provider training key. Both sources use advisory language and describe no enforcement mechanism. The supplied materials cite no FDA, ONC, civil-rights, or state statutory requirement for multilingual AI training.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares multilingual or multi-format AI training with single-language training on outcomes such as user error rates, override accuracy, or patient harm. The field also lacks baseline data on how often language mismatch between training materials and users leads to AI misuse in clinical settings.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The recommendation targets a language barrier directly, but its value for these groups remains unmeasured, and health systems serving them have no outcome data to guide what formats or languages to prioritize.
